facts.claim: Ilya Repin, Reply of the Zaporozhian Cossacks, 1880–1891, oil on canvas, State Russian Museum, St Petersburg
The bald head seen from behind (centre) belongs to Georgy (Georgi) Alekseyev, an imperial court official, who refused to pose for it (Wikipedia: he felt it was undignified)

Repin sketched the back of his head while he was distracted (hedged 'the story goes': Vokrug Sveta says Yavornytsky showed the numismatist his coin collection; Wikipedia says he was looking at prints)
Repin reportedly exclaimed 'It takes centuries to create a head like that!' (translated from Russian: 'Нужны века, чтоб создать такой затылок!'; paraphrased and hedged)
When he saw the painting, Alekseyev recognised his head and was not pleased
The historian Dmytro Yavornytsky, Repin's consultant and friend, posed for the scribe
The Cossacks who posed were Repin's friends and acquaintances (Yavornytsky, General Dragomirov as Sirko, Rubets, Tarnovsky, Fyodor Stravinsky…): 'almost every face'

caption:
This bald head was painted without its owner's consent.

In the middle of Ilya Repin's Reply of the Zaporozhian Cossacks (1880–1891), one Cossack turns his back to us: a shining bald head. It belonged to Georgy Alekseyev, an imperial court official, who refused to pose. The story goes that while he was distracted (Repin's friend, the historian Dmytro Yavornytsky, showed him a collection), Repin quickly sketched the back of his head. Repin is said to have exclaimed that a head like that takes centuries to make. When Alekseyev saw the finished painting, he recognised his own head, and he was not pleased.

Almost every face in that laughing crowd is a real person from Repin's life: Yavornytsky is the scribe, General Dragomirov is the ataman Sirko.

🎬 The whole story is a film on our YouTube channel: “These Men Are Laughing at an Emperor”

🖤 Would you have let him paint you?
